name: Pattern 6: Language Access
title: Pattern 6: Language Access
answer: Language Access is the sixth of ten patterns that recur across AI in schools: using AI to translate school communication so families and students who speak a language other than English receive it in a language they read comfortably. It matters because it can open school communication to families for the first time, but translation errors carry real risk, so messages must be sorted by stakes and higher-stakes messages checked by a fluent person or trained interpreter.

crumbs.name: Ten Patterns That Show Up Everywhere

sections.body: This pattern covers the use of AI to translate a newsletter, convert a teacher's message into a family's home language, or give an English learner a science reading in simpler words. The problem it solves is that many families have never received school communication in a language they read comfortably, and AI can change that. The same tool that widens access can also mislead, because translation quality varies with sentence length, language, and subject matter. The pattern therefore pairs the benefit with a caution: the value is hard to overstate, and so are the risks when translation goes wrong. It treats translation as a way to reach families, not as a replacement for human judgment about what a message means.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, the pattern works by sorting messages according to how much is at stake. Low-stakes items, such as a reminder about picture day, can go out through a translation tool with little risk. High-stakes items, such as a notice about special education services, discipline, or a health emergency, should be checked by a fluent person or handled by a trained interpreter. The text does not give separate grade-band versions of this practice; it describes the sorting rule as something any front office can follow, and notes that Chapter 14 builds it into a simple chart. The same sorting applies to classroom materials, where an English learner may receive a science reading in simpler words.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text labels this pattern with evidence drawn from reviews outside education. A review from health care, where translation errors can be dangerous, found that machine translation should be treated as a first draft followed by human correction (Dew et al., 2018). A later review found serious errors in many studies and lower accuracy for languages such as Haitian Creole and Vietnamese (Strechen et al., 2025). The text adds that schools serve families who speak both widely spoken European languages and languages like these. It also states that machine translation works best on short, simple sentences and on widely spoken European languages.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits are set by how translation fails: accuracy drops for longer or more complex sentences and for languages such as Haitian Creole and Vietnamese, and reviews have found serious errors. The risk is highest where a mistranslation could affect services, discipline, or health, so those messages stay with a fluent person or a trained interpreter rather than the tool alone. Machine translation is treated as a first draft that a human corrects, not as a final product. The decision about which messages are low stakes and which are high stakes remains with school staff, and the text points to a chart any front office can follow rather than leaving the sorting to the tool.
